name: Freya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll answer as best I can.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five, check the robot milker's overnight report on the herd app, then walk through the cows with Greg, our herdsman. Then it's calves, feeding, any sick cows, and the vet if needed. I love the calves; what wears me out is the milk buyer's paperwork and the inspections.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hillhead is my husband Callum's family farm, 160 hectares and 220 dairy cows, with grass and maize. I studied agriculture, met Callum at college, and I've run the herd for fifteen years. We've got Ruth, who's thirteen, and James, who's ten, and a mortgage on the house we built when Callum's parents kept the old farmhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we were right not to rush. We waited till three neighbours had a robotic milker before we got ours in 2024, and that's how I'd treat AI too. I'd say it at the young farmers' club, where I help run things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we keep on as we are, which is a good place. Hillhead is my husband Callum's family farm, 220 dairy cows on 160 hectares of grass and maize. I run the herd and Callum runs the fields, and the milk cheque is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the second robotic milker we've been planning, about 150,000, with a loan and savings, in spring 2027. I'd keep using the herd app that flags lame or sick cows. Otherwise it's the same work, the same buyer and the same herdsman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My worries are the milk price and Callum's dad's health. AI doesn't come into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you waited for three neighbours. Why three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One neighbour could be lucky, two could be stubborn, but three neighbours means a new machine works. The Morrisons, the Hendersons and the Kerrs all had robots for at least a year before we did. I went and stood in all three sheds and asked the cows, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think about at work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greg, our herdsman, who's been with us six years. Greg was worried the robot would take his job in 2024, and instead it took the night milking off him. In this picture, Greg carries on and maybe gets a little more time off.

say: I'd say we were **right not to rush**, as with our robotic milker.
I'd say it at the **young farmers' club**, where I help run things.
think: I think we **keep on** as we are, which is a good place.
The **milk cheque** is steady, with me on the herd and Callum on the fields.
do: Get the **second robotic milker** in spring 2027 for about 150,000.
Keep using the **herd app** that flags lame or sick cows.
feel: **Calm**, with only the usual worries about **milk price** and family health.
S0.quote: One neighbour could be lucky, two could be stubborn, but three neighbours means a new machine works.
fieldNote: She is **steady**: she buys new kit once three neighbours have proven it.

She remembers **Greg**, the herdsman, fearing the robot milker in 2024.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing, and dairies will be fine. Farming is hands-on, and we've already got some robots. I'd tell the young farmers to learn the tools but keep their hands dirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's a small help for us. The milk buyer's paperwork, the feed orders and the vet records would get easier. I'd use it once the other farms have, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the second robot milker on schedule in 2027. I'd let the milk buyer's AI system plan our feed and orders once a couple of neighbours say it works. And I'd go on the dairy co-op's day course on herd software next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of change I can manage. It helps more than it hurts us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell the young farmers to keep their hands dirty. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean the ones who only know the screen can't tell when a cow is off her food by looking at her eyes. The app tells you the yield is down, but a good stockman knows why before the app does. That's what I'd want them to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your family this would affect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's sister, Anne, works in the council's planning office. Anne's job is exactly the kind this picture changes, all forms and checking. I'd tell her she could always come and help on the farm, though she'd laugh at me.

I'd tell young farmers to learn the tools but keep their **hands dirty**.
think: I think it's a **small help** for us with paperwork and orders.
I'd use it **once other farms** have, like always.

feel: **Calm**, seeing it as a change she can **manage**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and that's not good for anyone. Farmers need time to see what works. I'd say at church and at the club that families need to look after each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right, because we own the farm and we've already got robots in the parlour. The bigger dairies would buy fleets and push the milk price down, so we'd earn less. But we wouldn't lose the farm, and I don't think I'd lose my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build savings to eighteen months of costs straight away. I'd wait to see the first full robot dairies, probably by 2031, then copy what works on a neighbour's farm. And I'd talk to Ruth and James about what they might do, because farming might need fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. We'd be fine, but the village wouldn't be the same. I'd worry about the young farmers more than us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives first, then the robots three years later. How does that work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the herd records and the ordering go to AI, which I'd half welcome. The robots in 2031 are the bigger change, but we've got a head start with the milkers. Those three years are when I'd watch the neighbours closely and pick the robots that actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about the young farmers. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben, at the club, is nineteen and just started as a tractor driver on the big arable estate. The young farmers' club has a lad called Ben with no land and no savings, and a robot tractor would take his job. I'd tell Ben to get an apprenticeship fixing the robots, because that's where the work would be.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and farmers need time to see what works.
I'd say at church that **families** must look after each other.
think: I think we'd be **all right**, owning the farm with robots in the parlour.
Bigger dairies would push the **milk price** down, so we'd earn less.
do: Build savings to **eighteen months** of costs straight away.

Talk to **Ruth and James** about careers if farming needs fewer people.
feel: **Uneasy**, sure the family is fine but the **village** will change.
S2.quote: The young farmers' club has a lad called Ben with no land and no savings, and a robot tractor would take his job.
fieldNote: She feels **protected** by owning the farm and having robot milkers already.
Her worry shifts to the **village** and young workers like Ben.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as with the fast one, I'd say families and communities need to stick together. Five years is better for farmers, but still quick. I'd say it calmly at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for us to switch at our own pace. We'd add robots as they're proven, maybe one a year after 2031. The milk price would fall, but we'd keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep the second robot plan. I'd watch the robot farms for a year or two before buying more. And I'd set up an apprenticeship scheme at the young farmers' club with the robot dealer, so lads like Ben get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. Five years is enough time to see what's coming. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting up an apprenticeship scheme. Is that something you've done before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not exactly, but I organised the club's stock-judging training for twenty young people last year. It's the same idea: find someone who knows, and get the young ones in front of them. The robot dealer would be glad of trained people anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Callum's parents say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's father would grumble that the cows need people, and Callum's mother would say she always knew it'd come. My husband Callum's parents milked by hand when they started, so they've seen big changes before. They'd want to know the farm stays in the family, that's all.

I'd say five years is **better**, but still quick for farmers.
think: I think five years lets us switch at **our own pace**.
We'd add **one robot a year** after 2031 and keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair time, and farming has adapted to bigger things. I'd say we should use it to train young people properly. I'd be fairly positive about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is comfortable for us. I'd be 56 in 2039, the farm would be mostly robots by then, and Callum and I would be running it, not doing all the work. I think it'd be a good life, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, with the second robot in 2027. I'd plan for more robots slowly, as they prove themselves, through the 2030s. And I'd encourage Ruth, who loves the cows, to think about taking on the farm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long, slow change we can manage. We'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years gives Ruth time to grow up. What would you want for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Ruth to go to agricultural college first, like I did, and then decide. If she comes back to Hillhead, she'd be running a robot dairy, which is a different job from mine. But she'd still need to know cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people would forget how to farm by hand. If the robots broke down for a week, who'd know how to milk 220 cows? I'd want Ruth and James both to learn the old way, just in case.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to see what works before we had to decide. What would help is time, and proper apprenticeships for young people to learn the new trades. Not handouts, but real training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about our faith. When things change fast, people lean on each other, and our church does that well. That matters more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: When things change fast, people lean on each other, and our church does that well.
portrait: Freya, 43, runs the **dairy herd** on her husband's family farm, with a robotic milker since 2024.
She is **steady**: she waits until three neighbours have proven a machine.
She values **community** and apprenticeships over government help.
She stays **calm or uneasy** in every picture, protected by ownership and early robots.
Her worry shifts to **young workers** like Ben in the village.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as there'd be no time to see what works.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and proper **apprenticeships** for young people to learn new trades.
